lessons.title: LLDB, diagnostic boundaries, and Objective-C interoperability
lessons.summary: Use LLDB to answer one precise question. Check where execution stopped, which values you inspected, and which binary and language boundary produced the result.
objectives: Describe a debugging question and collect its stop reason, frame, values, and loaded binary.
Tell apart reading stored state and running a debugger expression, especially in optimized code.
Follow the headers, selectors, and optional values that connect Swift with Objective-C.
Write a report that identifies the artifact and check instead of assuming every failure is a cache problem.

sections.title: Start with a question you can check
sections.html:
An invariant is a rule that should keep holding, such as one tap causing one increment. You already use Android Studio to ask why a field changed or a callback ran twice. Bring one such question to LLDB, Xcode’s debugger. State the expected transition: one increment, no callback after its owner stops, or an offline error kept distinct from empty success. A breakpoint, which pauses execution at a chosen place, is useful when it captures the point where that rule may fail.

Write the reproduction inputs, selected app or test host, scheme action, configuration, destination, and expected event order. A Debug build can be easier to inspect, but a Release-only bug may require the optimized artifact. A simulator observation has a simulator scope. A crash report from a distributed device build needs that build's symbols, rather than symbols from whichever checkout currently opens in Xcode.

Choose synthetic state when practicing and inspect only the fields needed to decide the hypothesis. Printing an entire account object, request, preference store, or environment is unnecessary and can expose sensitive information. The repository anchors here show real Objective-C and Swift integration points, but the exercise runs only in your own scratch code if you choose to execute it. Source inspection does not establish that an app has paused in LLDB or that a production crash has been reproduced.

sections.title: Check why and where the program stopped
sections.html:
A stack frame is one call in the chain that led to the current stop. First read the stop reason, thread, and selected frame. One source line may cover several machine instructions, and one function breakpoint may have several locations. An unresolved breakpoint may mean symbols are missing, paths differ, code was not compiled into this artifact, or optimization changed its shape. It does not prove the callback never runs. Check the loaded code before drawing that conclusion.

# Enter these in LLDB's console, not the shell.
help breakpoint set
breakpoint set --file CourseCounter.swift --line 8
breakpoint list
thread backtrace
thread backtrace all
frame variable
frame variable count

Help uses the installed debugger's command documentation. The file and line are synthetic placeholders to replace with your scratch source. Breakpoint list shows whether locations resolved. Thread backtrace describes the selected thread; adding all gathers other threads. Frame variable reads values in the selected frame using debug information. It does not universally guarantee every local remains available in optimized code. Inspect the intended frame before concluding that a missing variable is a compiler or runtime defect.

Stepping over stays at the current call level; stepping into follows a call where symbols and code permit; stepping out returns to the caller. Suspension and concurrency complicate the familiar linear stack: an async operation may resume on another thread, and a thread is not an actor's identity. Use Xcode's task/concurrency views when appropriate and combine them with explicit state observations. Breakpoints change timing, so they are poor evidence for a performance measurement or for proving the absence of a race.

sections.title: Reading a value and evaluating code are different
sections.html:
Expression evaluation runs code through the debugger. Frame-variable inspection instead reads stored values using debug information. Commands such as p and po often use expressions or object descriptions. A computed property, formatter, custom description, or function can allocate, lock, or change state when evaluated. Start with stored fields if they answer your question. Then say explicitly when you choose to run a getter or another expression, because that action is part of the experiment.

final class CourseCounter {
    private(set) var count = 0

    func recordTap() {
        count += 1
    }

    var label: String {
        "Taps: \(count)"
    }
}

This ordinary Swift class is suitable for a standalone scratch program or host package. Private(set) allows callers to read count but limits mutation to the declaration's access context. The stored count starts at zero. RecordTap mutates it once. Label is a computed property and constructs a string every time it is evaluated. The interpolation reads count; it is not a stored snapshot. Set a breakpoint inside recordTap after constructing a counter and invoking the method from your scratch driver.

Inspect count, then deliberately evaluate label and explain why that second action executes a getter. Do not use expression to call recordTap unless your exercise explicitly intends to mutate the process. In a real program, getters may lock, allocate, or consult other state. A failed Swift expression can also reflect debugger module-import or type-context problems while the compiled program remains valid. Preserve that distinction and report the debugger failure separately from the application's observed behavior.

sections.title: Find the stage that produced the error
sections.html:
A diagnostic is a tool’s report of a problem. Identify its stage first. Swift type checking checks source. Linking joins compiled definitions. The dynamic loader finds separate binaries at launch. LLDB expressions have their own compile and evaluation context. Missing imports suggest products, target dependencies, platform support, or generated modules. Undefined symbols suggest missing or repeated definitions and linkage. A launch loader failure suggests embedding, run paths, slices, or signatures. The first useful diagnostic points to the next check.

# Shell inspection of the selected tools
xcode-select -p
xcrun --find swiftc
xcrun swift --version
xcodebuild -version

# LLDB inspection of loaded images
image list -u -f
image lookup -rn recordTap

The first group inspects tool selection and versions without claiming an app build. The second belongs in a stopped debugging session; UUIDs and paths connect symbols to the loaded artifact. The regular-expression lookup can find matching functions, subject to emitted symbols and optimization. A release crash needs matching dSYM UUIDs, not merely a matching marketing version or source filename.

Optimization can inline functions, remove variables, and move work relative to source lines. Debugging an unoptimized reproduction helps understanding but may change the failure. Preserve the optimized artifact when it is the relevant evidence. Use a bounded isolated cache or regeneration check only after identifying the graph and diagnostic. The repository notes a stale-DerivedData issue when switching build actions; that documented symptom does not establish that every missing symbol has the same cause.

For a worked symbol mismatch, compare UUID and architecture for the scratch executable, candidate dSYM, and crash image before interpreting a stack. A matching filename or version string is insufficient. In the artifact-debugging workshop, synthetic excerpts deliberately disagree on UUID; the next action is to find the matching retained artifact, not symbolicate against the nearest build. frame variable inspects stored state, while expression may execute code, including getters. A predicted LLDB transcript stays a prediction until an actual stopped process supplies it.

sections.title: Follow each direction between Swift and Objective-C
sections.html:
Interoperability means Swift and Objective-C can call compatible declarations across their language boundary. Each direction has its own path. In the app target, a bridging header exposes selected C and Objective-C headers to Swift through SWIFT_OBJC_BRIDGING_HEADER. The app’s header imports UIKit, CoreLocation, CoreData, and a C system header. Frameworks and packages commonly expose public headers as modules instead. ZDCoreObjc is one inspected target with explicit public-header membership. None of this automatically exposes all Swift declarations back to Objective-C.

In the other direction, the compiler generates a ProductModuleName-Swift.h interface for Objective-C-compatible Swift declarations. Objective-C implementation files import the relevant generated interface according to the app or framework context. Do not hand-edit that generated header, and avoid header cycles by keeping imports and forward declarations in appropriate places. A missing generated header can arise from product module name, target membership, build order, or unsupported declarations rather than from the Swift file's spelling.

Nullability says whether an Objective-C object may be absent. A nullable result generally imports as a Swift optional; an unspecified declaration can leave less safe assumptions. Inspect the generated interface instead of guessing. Foundation values can bridge, but arbitrary Swift structs, associated-value enums, and generic APIs are not all representable in Objective-C. NSError conventions may import as throwing Swift calls. An Objective-C exception is different: ordinary Swift do/catch is not its recovery boundary. Treat these failure mechanisms separately.

sections.title: Check callback names and UI ownership separately
sections.html:
A selector names an Objective-C method and its argument positions. UIKit target/action uses it to find a callback; it is not a Swift closure. BindableTapGestureRecognizer registers self with #selector and exposes the callback with @objc. It also stores a closure, which creates a separate ownership question. The selector does not make that closure weak or cancel its work. Check the callback signature, retained owner, captures, and Swift isolation rule as separate parts of the interaction.

import UIKit

@MainActor
final class CourseTapTarget: NSObject {
    private(set) var count = 0

    func configure(_ button: UIButton) {
        button.addTarget(
            self,
            action: #selector(didTap(_:)),
            for: .touchUpInside
        )
    }

    @objc private func didTap(_ sender: UIButton) {
        count += 1
        sender.setTitle("Taps: \(count)", for: .normal)
    }
}

This requires an iOS UIKit target and a caller that retains CourseTapTarget for the interaction lifetime. It is not a complete screen. The underscore in configure removes its external argument label. The selector includes an underscore placeholder for one argument, corresponding to the Objective-C method's colon. @objc exposes a representable method, even though Swift access is private. NSObject supplies an Objective-C-compatible class base.

MainActor states the Swift isolation rule for UI work. It does not automatically move an arbitrary Objective-C call from a background thread to that actor. Check the real callback context and adapt legacy callers through an explicit boundary. An Android listener helps explain registering a callback, but it does not explain selectors, generated headers, or Objective-C method lookup. A selector breakpoint may help find calls; do not assume the Swift source spelling is the complete runtime symbol name.

sections.title: Choose a tool for the kind of failure
sections.html:
An exception is an Objective-C runtime failure mechanism, separate from a thrown Swift Error. Xcode’s exception breakpoint can stop when one is raised, such as an unrecognized selector. A Swift Error breakpoint can stop at an expected error that will later be caught. That stop is not proof of a crash. Traps, failed preconditions, and fatalError follow another path. Name the mechanism and inspect the first relevant application frame before treating a red console line as the cause.

Memory Graph helps inspect retained objects and references. Zombies helps investigate messages to deallocated Objective-C objects, changing normal deallocation behavior. Address Sanitizer targets memory-access errors; Thread Sanitizer targets data races; Main Thread Checker flags certain UI API misuse. Their availability, overhead, and supported destination constraints differ. Choose according to the hypothesis and consult the selected Xcode's diagnostics; no single switch proves ownership, actor correctness, or all memory safety.

The retained production scheme disables Main Thread Checker for its launch action and enables Zombies as an additional test option. Those are current scheme declarations, not ideal defaults to copy into every exercise and not proof that a particular run used them. The active source also has DEBUG-gated diagnostics. Compiler conditions decide whether code exists; diagnostic run options decide instrumentation; runtime feature flags decide behavior in the existing binary. Keep these three categories separate. For performance checks, record instrumentation and debugger attachment because they can change the phenomenon being measured.

sections.title: Write what the debugger actually showed
sections.html:
A debugging report should let another engineer assess your conclusion. Include the rule you expected, reproduction steps, artifact identity, stop reason, selected frame, and only the values needed for the question. For CourseCounter, one call changes count from 0 to 1. Observing a second call would support duplicate delivery. Finding count equal to 2 without observing the calls does not identify the caller or registration that caused it. Keep that uncertainty in the report.

For an interoperability failure, attach the declared callback signature, its selector or generated interface, target membership, and loaded-image evidence. If a nullable result was treated as present, explain the imported optionality and the point where it was unwrapped. If a macro-generated module fails only in expression evaluation, retain the compiler's successful build evidence separately from LLDB's failed expression. This prevents a debugger limitation from being misreported as a platform defect.

Use the smallest safe experiment to resolve the uncertainty. A pure class can be debugged on the host; a UIKit selector requires a suitable iOS target; an account or device SDK problem needs its own authorized integration environment. Report unexecuted checks as pending. The worked exercise provides predictions and an inspection order, without claiming that source reading reproduced a crash, validated the installed toolchain, or completed specialist Objective-C runtime analysis. Knowing that boundary is part of being ready to debug a production codebase.

quiz.question: Why inspect a stored field before evaluating a computed property in LLDB?
options: Stored-value inspection can answer the question without deliberately executing the getter.
Computed properties never exist in Release.
LLDB expressions are always read-only.
Only private values can be printed.
quiz.explanation: Expression/getter evaluation can run code and affect timing or state. Stored debug-information inspection is a better first step when it suffices, though optimization and formatters still require care.

quiz.question: What does @objc on a callback establish?
options: The stored closure captures weakly.
A representable declaration is exposed to Objective-C dispatch.
A background caller is automatically moved to MainActor.
Every Swift generic becomes visible to Objective-C.
quiz.explanation: Objective-C exposure, capture lifetime, actor isolation, and representability are separate contracts. #selector chooses the exposed method; it does not repair threading or ownership.

quiz.question: An app builds, but LLDB cannot evaluate a Swift expression. What should the report say?
options: The app source is necessarily invalid.
All caches must be deleted immediately.
The debugger's expression/module context failed; application behavior needs separate evidence.
The provisioning profile is certainly expired.
quiz.explanation: Debugger expression compilation has its own context. Preserve the actual successful build and runtime observations while investigating symbols, module imports, and toolchain compatibility.

exercise.brief: Debug or paper-trace CourseCounter in scratch work. Then explain the UIKit callback example and classify four interoperability failures.
steps: Predict count before and after one recordTap call. Say why label is computed rather than stored.
Optionally pause inside recordTap in a scratch host program. Record stop reason, frame, count, and loaded binary; otherwise label the trace as a prediction.

Read the bridging-header and gesture-recognizer anchors. Follow @objc, #selector, the stored closure, and the retained owner.

Executed observations include artifact/configuration/stop scope; paper traces remain labeled predictions.

exercise.solution:
A fresh counter starts at 0. One recordTap call changes it to 1, and the computed label then returns Taps: 1. If you run the scratch program, break on the actual source line inside recordTap. Check the selected frame, then inspect count before and after stepping over the increment. Evaluating label runs its getter. Calling recordTap through a debugger expression would add another tap and alter the experiment. These outputs remain predictions until you record a real stopped process.

For the UIKit example, an owner must retain CourseTapTarget. Configure removes its external argument label, #selector(didTap(_:)) identifies a one-argument Objective-C method, and @objc exposes that method. MainActor requires appropriate UI access, while Objective-C exposure alone supplies no automatic thread hop. The active gesture source additionally stores a closure, whose captures need an independent ownership review.

A nil imported result suggests checking nullability and optional handling. An unrecognized selector suggests callback signature and Objective-C exposure. A missing generated Swift header suggests target/module identity and build membership. Mismatched release symbols require the actual binary's UUID-matching dSYMs. Host counter results do not validate UIKit delivery or a production crash; keep those observations pending unless executed in their proper targets.

lessons.title: Test, CI, destination, and configuration matrices
lessons.summary: Plan tests for the exact build, destination, and behavior a change affects. Record what ran, what was skipped, and which products supplied the evidence.
objectives: Keep build settings, test-plan options, destination, runtime data, and build route in separate fields.
Read the current CI workflows and test plans for both retained and Tuist build routes.
Choose host, simulator, device, extension, and package checks for the changed behavior.
Record test counts, skips, retries, cache inputs, and artifacts so another engineer can repeat the checks.

sections.title: Give every result a build and a destination
sections.html:
A test matrix is a table of the checks chosen for a change. An Android prodNormalDebug unit test does not establish release shrinking or another flavor’s behavior. An iOS result likewise belongs to a source revision, dependencies, toolchain, scheme action, build configuration, test plan, destination, and fixture set. A fixture is controlled test input. Name these choices so “tests passed” says what passed and where. Otherwise, the result cannot support a precise release decision.

Start from the changed contract. A pure parsing rule needs deterministic model tests. A UIKit resource change needs the relevant target and bundle lookup. A shared core dependency can reach an app, App Clip, widget, or test host. A compiler macro needs a host-tool path in addition to consumer compilation. An authentication SDK change needs account, cancellation, and device integration cases. This is a risk-based matrix, not a demand to run every possible Cartesian product for every edit.

The checkout has both retained-workspace and generated Tuist workflows. Neither path's existence proves the other is retired. Read the actual trigger and build commands, then associate results with the path exercised. This session extends session 026's artifact ledger into test selection and reproducibility. The worked matrix is a planning tool until you attach actual results; reading a workflow is evidence of configured automation, not proof that a particular job ran or passed.

sections.title: Separate build settings from test-plan options
sections.html:
A build configuration controls compilation and linking, as Debug and Release do. A test-plan configuration instead varies runner options such as arguments, environment, language, region, or diagnostics. Selecting one does not automatically select a different build configuration. A Run action’s environment is also not necessarily the Test action’s environment, or the environment of an app started by a UI test. Give these choices separate fields before deciding which combinations the change needs.

A destination adds platform, device or simulator type, architecture, and runtime. An arm64 simulator and arm64 device require different binaries. The deployment minimum is not the installed simulator version. A successful test on the newest available runtime does not demonstrate correctness on the app's oldest supported runtime. SDK compilation and runtime availability tests answer different questions, as session 044 explained.

AxisExampleWhat it changes
Graph routeRetained workspace or TuistManifests, products, generated settings, pins
Build configurationDebug or ReleaseConditions, optimization, testability, linking
Test plan/configurationUnit plan with locale optionSelected tests and runner options
DestinationSimulator runtime/devicePlatform, architecture, execution environment
Runtime fixturesOffline or synthetic accountProduct behavior under controlled inputs

Use a separate cell for every distinction that matters to the change. Combining all choices into a name such as production test build can conceal that DEBUG and PROD conditions coexist, or that a UI test uses a synthetic runtime override. Inspect the final product's settings and the runner's launch configuration instead of inferring them from the matrix row's title.

sections.title: Read the workflow and the selected plan
sections.html:
A CI workflow describes automated steps; it does not prove those steps ran. The inspected toolchain workflow selects Xcode 26.5 and an iPhone 17 Pro Max simulator at version 26.5. These are checkout pins, not claims about your installed machine or the latest tools. The Tuist workflow installs dependencies, runs post-clone setup, generates the workspace, builds for testing, and tests without building. Its commands select ZocdocUnitTests, disable selective testing, and share a destination.

The retained pull-request workflow uses Zocdoc.xcworkspace and the Zocdoc Prod scheme. It computes test shards using timing inputs, builds for testing, and then runs a selected plan and filter arguments without rebuilding. It has explicit unit-failure and UI-retry branches and saves result artifacts. The Tuist workflow also has a pull_request trigger in the inspected file. Therefore historical guide wording that PR CI only builds the retained path is not sufficient to describe the current configured automation.

Read the actual ZocdocUnitTests.xctestplan rather than stopping at the app scheme's older single-target comment. The current plan includes many package test targets as well as the app-hosted tests. It also has explicit skipped Swift Testing suites/functions and XCTest classes/methods. A stale comment about intended aggregation should not shrink your coverage claim, while a listed target still needs result evidence to prove it executed. This distinction is particularly useful during a generator migration, when plans, target identifiers, and workflow names can drift independently.

sections.title: Build test products, then run those same products
sections.html:
Build-for-testing compiles the app and tests and prepares metadata that describes how to run them. It does not execute tests. Test-without-building uses those prepared products. Separating the two can save compilation time, but they must refer to compatible products and execution settings. If source, manifests, conditions, resources, or compiler inputs change, rebuild the affected products. Reusing whichever output happens to be in DerivedData does not establish that the intended change was tested.

# Discovery from an already prepared retained client checkout:
xcodebuild -list -workspace Zocdoc.xcworkspace
xcodebuild -showdestinations -workspace Zocdoc.xcworkspace -scheme "Zocdoc Prod"

# Template mirroring the pinned Tuist workflow; not executed here:
# COURSE_DESTINATION must describe an inspected available simulator.
tuist test ZocdocUnitTests --build-only --no-selective-testing --configuration Debug -- -destination "$COURSE_DESTINATION"
tuist test ZocdocUnitTests --without-building --no-selective-testing -- -destination "$COURSE_DESTINATION"

The discovery commands can require prepared dependency state, and they do not prove a build. The template's variable is task-specific, not a repurposed system path. The double dash forwards following options to the underlying Xcode build command in this pinned workflow. Use the repository's build instructions and installed-version help before operational execution. Generated support files and setup are required inputs, so the template is not a promise that a fresh unauthenticated checkout can run immediately.

The Tuist workflow explicitly avoids globally disabling signing for simulator test hosts because Keychain tests rely on entitlement context. Do not copy CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO into every row. An isolated pure package and an app-hosted test have different requirements. Save separate build and execution results, and report a build failure as such rather than marking every unexecuted test as failed behavior.

sections.title: Choose checks for the affected boundaries
sections.html:
Coverage here means the behavior and combinations your evidence actually checks. Begin a dependency change with the smallest affected unit tests, then add consumers on the supported CI route. If the app minimum is iOS 17, a compatibility claim needs a justified check on that minimum runtime or a stated gap when it is unavailable. The current CI simulator pin cannot supply that proof. Add iPad or size cases when layout or resources change; one phone picture cannot cover them all.

RowPurposeLimit
Host pure model testsValue/error contractNo UIKit or app packaging
Tuist Debug simulator planGenerated graph integrationNo production device archive
Retained Debug unit/UI plansCoexistence consumersSelected tests and destination only
Release device build/package reviewOptimized linkage and resource inclusionExecution/distribution still separate
Affected extension or App ClipCapability and shared dependency boundaryOnly named product verified
Minimum/runtime-specific casesAvailability and compatibilityRequires an available appropriate runtime/device

Some rows can be compile-only; others need execution, resource lookup, installation, or archive inspection. Label the evidence type. Include locale, dynamic text, offline behavior, synthetic account transition, or cancellation only when the change affects those contracts. A security SDK or media update warrants specialized device tests. Pairwise sampling can reduce combinations, but it is a strategy with stated exclusions, not a mathematical guarantee that every important interaction was tested.

sections.title: Count selected, skipped, and retried tests
sections.html:
Test discovery is the step that finds runnable tests. A manifest target may not be in the selected scheme. A plan entry may be skipped or excluded by filters. A compiled test may fail discovery because of framework conventions or target membership. Compare expected and observed test counts. Record plans, filters, skips, failures, and retries. A successful command that ran zero intended tests does not establish that the behavior passed. Parallel execution adds its own fixture-ownership questions.

The plan represents skipped Swift Testing suites or functions separately from XCTest classes or methods. It marks the app-hosted target nonparallelizable; other targets have their own settings. Within-process test execution and Xcode distributing runners are different controls. One nonparallel target setting does not prove every shared fixture is safe. Prefer a fixture owned by its test, or use an explicit actor or synchronization rule. Then record the discovered and executed cases rather than relying on the setting alone.

The retained workflow retries selected UI failures after resetting simulator state and preserves result bundles. A retry success can establish eventual execution success while still leaving a flakiness concern. Keep the first failure, retry input, and final result in the ledger. Do not replace an invariant with a larger sleep or silently remove the failing row. Quarantine is an explicit maintenance decision with scope and ownership, not something inferred from a green aggregate icon. The intentionally skipped CI canary in the plan demonstrates why skip-list correctness itself can be a tested operational boundary.

sections.title: Name the inputs behind a reused output
sections.html:
A cache key identifies the inputs used to choose reusable material. The Tuist dependency cache hashes Package.swift, Package.resolved, and mise.toml, with Xcode in relevant keys. The Tuist/.build scratch restore has no broad fallback. The content-addressed shared cache can use a prefix restore. These stores have different rules: verified source revisions may be reusable, while stale mutable resolution state can break generation or select the wrong graph. Identify the cache before deciding to clear or trust it.

Tuist.swift separately states that the Xcode compilation cache is off, while the Tuist module cache remains a different mechanism. Do not collapse dependency caches, compiler caches, generated projects, DerivedData, and remote module artifacts into one instruction to clear the cache. Identify which inputs feed the questionable artifact and preserve failure evidence before trying a narrow clean reproduction. A cache miss can be expected after a graph change; a cache hit is not proof of correct selection.

Reproducibility means another suitable environment can reconstruct the intended graph and interpret the result from the recorded inputs. It does not promise identical signed bytes across machines. Record the commit, selected dependency revisions, compiler, generator, generated inputs, configuration, SDK and architecture, plan, and filters. Add artifact UUIDs when matching symbols. Keep credentials outside the record. If generation or resolution changes, inspect that diff before assuming a later failure came from application source.

sections.title: Separate planned checks from accepted results
sections.html:
An evidence record says what was planned, run, and accepted. A row is executed only when a real run supplies output. It is accepted only when that output meets the stated rule. A workflow file shows configured behavior. Compile success shows compilation in that context. A passing test shows its selected assertions. None automatically proves installation, privacy, or performance. Keep unavailable environments and pending specialist reviews visible so the next engineer knows what remains to decide.

Keep the handoff small but complete: the changed contract, affected graph rows, actual commands or run identifiers, results and artifacts, skipped/pending cases, and the owner of the next decision. An xcresult retains detailed test evidence, while an archive and matching symbols serve a different purpose. Include original failure and retry evidence if a job eventually passed. A screenshot supports visible state at one time, not an unobserved lifecycle or network guarantee.

The course author's inspection of workflows and plans is separate from the learner's exercise execution. The worked answer below deliberately leaves real client rows pending. Session 049 combines this ledger with a bounded change and reconstruction plan. Learning to say precisely what was checked is the transferable skill: it allows a reviewer to assess residual risk without either overclaiming completion or rerunning every possible test because the original evidence was too vague.

An explicit matrix row reads “Release / app plus affected extension / selected device SDK / compile and package-resource review / result pending.” Another reads “Debug / host contract target / selected plan / executed test count and fixture results.” Those rows cannot substitute for one another. The artifact-debugging workshop supplies an investigation sequence and synthetic membership failure; the native target is SwiftUIWorkbench and the language host is SwiftLanguageLab. Attach actual destinations, discovered/skipped cases, result bundles, and runtime outcomes only after execution.

quiz.question: What does build-for-testing establish by itself?
options: The selected test products compiled and execution metadata was prepared.
All listed tests ran.
Device installation and archive export succeeded.
The oldest supported OS passed.
quiz.explanation: Execution belongs to the following test phase, and device/archive/minimum-runtime claims require their own rows. Keep build and test evidence separate.

quiz.question: How should the current Tuist plan's coverage be described?
options: Use the older single-target scheme comment without reading the plan.
The inspected plan lists app and package targets; actual execution and skips still need results.
Every target in the repository automatically runs.
Swift Testing skips are identical to XCTest method identifiers.
quiz.explanation: Current plan data outweighs stale aggregation comments. Listed coverage is configured coverage; results, filters, and framework-specific skips determine executed coverage.

quiz.question: A failed UI test passes on retry. What belongs in the ledger?
options: Only the final green icon.
Original failure, retry selection, final result, and remaining flakiness concern.
A claim that timing cannot affect the test.
Removal of the test from all future plans.
quiz.explanation: Eventual success and reliability are different facts. Preserving both runs supports diagnosis and an explicit maintenance decision rather than hiding the first failure.

exercise.brief: Plan checks for a synthetic shared-resource dependency change that reaches an app and one extension. Run only isolated fixtures if you choose to execute part of the plan.
steps: Read both CI routes, their toolchain pins, the current Tuist plan, and the retained scheme’s test plans.
Choose six rows: pure contract, generated consumer, retained consumer, Release packaging, affected extension, and minimum-runtime behavior.
For each row, name build settings, test-plan options, destination, fixtures, evidence type, and passing outcome.
State which inputs must match between build-for-testing and test-without-building. Include expected test-discovery counts.
Mark unrun client rows pending. Explain how skips, filters, and retries limit the result.
acceptance: Rows distinguish graph route, build configuration, test plan/options, destination, and fixtures.
Minimum-runtime compatibility is not inferred from the current CI simulator pin.
A source-only audit is labeled configured evidence, and no client build or test is fabricated.
App/extension packaging and pure contract tests have different acceptance evidence.
The handoff includes test counts/filters/skips/retries, matching product identity, and cache inputs.
exercise.solution:
Use six checks with different purposes. Host fixtures check the resource rule. Tuist Debug simulator tests check generated consumers. Retained Debug tests check the other route’s consumers. A Release device build and package review check optimized linkage and resource inclusion. The affected extension needs its own build and lookup path. A minimum-supported-runtime check needs an appropriate environment. Add language or size cases when the resource changes UI. This is a planned matrix until actual outputs are attached.

The current workflow pins Xcode and simulator 26.5, while the app manifest's floor is iOS 17. Those numbers describe different axes. The current Tuist plan lists package targets despite older single-target prose. Both are declared observations, not executed results. A report should say client matrix pending unless actual run artifacts are supplied.

The pairing contract keeps source revision, pins, toolchain, configuration, architecture/SDK, generated resources, and managed build-product location compatible between build and execution. Compare expected tests with discovered/executed tests, account for explicit skips, and retain first-failure and retry bundles. A resource lookup passing on the host establishes only that package fixture; it does not accept the extension's device packaging, signing context, or distribution artifact.

simple.story: Asha tests a raincoat by pouring water over its sleeve. The sleeve stays dry inside. She writes that result down. She has not yet tested the zip, hood, or seams. Her friend tests a second coat in a different size. Both tests are useful, but neither says every coat is waterproof. Asha labels each result with the coat, part, and test used. When the zip changes, she checks the zip and the nearby seams rather than repeating unrelated size checks blindly.
simple.meaning: A test result belongs to particular source, tools, settings, destination, and inputs. Choose checks for the affected contract, and keep planned rows separate from actual results.

lessons.title: Bounded dependency and configuration change lab
lessons.summary: Practice one small package change: keep schema 1 working and accept schema 2 only with explicit opt-in. Preserve loader errors and rehearse two ways to undo the change.
objectives: Define a small change in behavior, dependencies, and compiler settings.
Add a local product to a scratch consumer and make its public API usable across modules.
Test accepted, rejected, and opt-in schema values separately from Debug and the service environment.
Record checks and recovery steps, keeping source reconstruction separate from fixing installed clients.

sections.title: Change one small acceptance rule
sections.html:
A schema is the structure and meaning a data format promises. This lab adds a small rule for which schema versions are accepted. Reuse the scratch CourseResources package from lesson 046 and add a sibling CoursePolicy package. It owns the acceptance rule. A separate compiler condition lets the consumer opt into the next schema. This is like separating an Android dependency, BuildConfig choice, and adapter behavior: record each change so a new result has an explainable cause.

The baseline accepts schema version 1 and rejects every other integer. The candidate accepts version 2 only when a deliberate opt-in is true. Invalid or future versions remain rejected. Missing files, I/O errors, and malformed JSON keep their original failure categories. The visible title and existing version-1 behavior remain stable. Write these invariants before implementation, because the tests should protect the product contract rather than count branches in your solution.

Work only in your own scratch packages or use a paper design if the needed toolchain is unavailable. The repository manifests are read-only evidence for how a real change would be reviewed. This exercise does not upgrade a client pin, rewrite an xcconfig, generate signing inputs, fetch a live schema, or distribute an app. Its worked answer is reference material, not a completed learner submission. Plan several short sessions for implementation, verification, and the final review note.

sections.title: Save the starting inputs and expected results
sections.html:
A baseline is the starting behavior you will compare with the candidate. Record the scratch revision or saved copy, tools version, directories, fixture, test names, and predicted results. CourseResources has title Course sandbox and schemaVersion 1. The lookup and missing-file tests from lesson 046 describe expected behavior. Assertions in a worked answer do not prove those tests passed. Put observed output or paper predictions in a separate column so your evidence keeps that distinction.

For the new package, identify a policy owner, a resource-loader consumer, and a graph maintainer. These are responsibilities in the exercise, not inferred company teams. The policy owner controls allowed versions; the consumer owns loading and user-facing error handling; the graph maintainer owns product selection and target dependencies. A real remote upgrade would additionally need selected-version provenance, transitive pin review, licenses, and relevant security review from session 044.

The active client keeps Package.swift and Project.swift side by side. For a future authorized client dependency edit, follow the documented manifest-sync workflow and verify both routes; modifying one input does not automatically update the other. The course lab does not dispatch that workflow because it changes no client manifests. Record this as a boundary in your review note. A good baseline ledger lets a reviewer distinguish an implementation failure from a graph, resource, or tool-selection failure.

sections.title: Make the small rule usable from another module
sections.html:
A public API contains declarations another module can use. Put the policy source under Sources/CoursePolicy in the new scratch package. It uses ordinary Swift with no UIKit, network, resources, or remote dependency. Its public modifiers matter because CourseResources is a different module. Internal declarations could pass tests inside CoursePolicy but fail at the actual consumer boundary. The rule should expose only an acceptance decision, leaving resource lookup and decoding with their current owner.

public enum SchemaDecision: Equatable {
    case accept
    case reject
}

public func schemaDecision(
    for version: Int,
    allowNext: Bool
) -> SchemaDecision {
    switch version {
    case 1:
        return .accept
    case 2:
        return allowNext ? .accept : .reject
    default:
        return .reject
    }
}

The enum defines the two decisions without exposing a vendor type. Equatable allows an expected-result assertion. The function's external for label makes the call read naturally; version is its local parameter. AllowNext is both an external label and local name. The exhaustive switch explicitly accepts version 1, gates version 2, and rejects every other integer. Its default is appropriate at an open input boundary: an unknown wire version must receive a deliberate rejection rule rather than being silently treated as current.

This function is deterministic and does not mutate shared state. A Kotlin sealed outcome or enum would be a useful analogy, but this Swift module's public declarations and library product determine cross-module visibility. It does not provide JSON decoding, resource lookup, remote flags, or authorization. Keeping the policy this small makes an adapter replacement or rollback review understandable without exposing the entire implementation of a third-party package.

sections.title: Declare the package and select its product
sections.html:
A product is the package output a target requests. Give CoursePolicy a tools-5.9 manifest with a library product for its source target and a separate test target. Then add the sibling package to the scratch CourseResources manifest and select its product in the resource target. Keep the resource declaration and test target. The partial declaration below shows only the changed fields. It describes the learner’s scratch graph, not a change to the client’s manifests.

// Changed fields inside the scratch CourseResources Package initializer:
dependencies: [
    .package(path: "../CoursePolicy")
],
targets: [
    .target(
        name: "CourseResources",
        dependencies: [
            .product(name: "CoursePolicy", package: "CoursePolicy")
        ],
        resources: [.process("Resources")]
    ),
    .testTarget(
        name: "CourseResourcesTests",
        dependencies: ["CourseResources"]
    )
]

The package dependency makes the sibling graph available. The target dependency grants the specific consumer access to the exported product. Its source still imports CoursePolicy. None of those steps substitutes for the others. Preserve the Resources declaration, because the code dependency does not move bootstrap.json into another bundle. Relative paths describe the scratch layout, not a remote version or lockfile entry for this local target.

Review the diff as a graph change: one new package, one product, one consuming edge, policy source/tests, and a consumer validation boundary. If unrelated pins, generated files, resources, or settings change, explain or remove those changes in your own lab before accepting the candidate. The real checkout's main app and extensions show why a small declaration can reach several products. Your scratch graph is intentionally narrow; successful compilation here does not prove parity for the production Tuist and retained-workspace routes.

sections.title: Keep opt-in separate from Debug and production
sections.html:
A compiler condition selects a source branch when building. This opt-in is COURSE_NEXT_SCHEMA. It is separate from DEBUG, PROD, the service environment, and a runtime flag. Debug can omit it; Release can deliberately include it. The client’s base configuration supplies PROD, while its Swift Debug list also supplies DEBUG. That proves these choices can coexist. Do not use Debug to mean sandbox, or production to mean optimized, without checking the actual settings and consumer.

var compiledAllowsNextSchema: Bool {
    #if COURSE_NEXT_SCHEMA
    return true
    #else
    return false
    #endif
}

This computed value converts a compile-time choice into a Boolean consumed by the pure policy. It does not read a server or change after installation. In a scratch SwiftPM consumer target you can add define for COURSE_NEXT_SCHEMA using that target's swiftSettings, then remove it to reconstruct the baseline. The setting must reach the consuming target; defining it only in CoursePolicy would not change this declaration in CourseResources.

Swift conditions and Objective-C preprocessor definitions are separate inputs. The active ZDFeatureFlags header enables its SSL-pinning diagnostic only when both DEBUG and TESTSECURE are defined. DEBUG by itself is not enough. A runtime experiment is another mechanism. This exercise changes neither trust settings nor client flags. It practices reading an AND rule and finding the target that consumes the condition. If you build, record the effective flags; a name written somewhere in the manifest is not proof it reached the compiler.

sections.title: Add schema rejection without erasing loader errors
sections.html:
Validation checks whether decoded data meets the product rule. It comes after resource lookup and decoding. In the scratch resource module, import CoursePolicy, call loadBootstrap, then ask the policy about schemaVersion. An unsupported schema gets a new typed error that records the rejected version. Keep missing files, I/O failures, and malformed JSON as their existing failures. They need different recovery. An empty successful value must not stand in for any of these rejected cases.

import CoursePolicy

enum ContractFailure: Error, Equatable {
    case unsupportedSchema(Int)
}

func validateSchema(_ version: Int, allowNext: Bool) throws {
    guard schemaDecision(for: version, allowNext: allowNext) == .accept else {
        throw ContractFailure.unsupportedSchema(version)
    }
}

func validatedBootstrap(
    named name: String = "bootstrap"
) throws -> CourseBootstrap {
    let value = try loadBootstrap(named: name)
    try validateSchema(value.schemaVersion, allowNext: compiledAllowsNextSchema)
    return value
}

The enum stores the rejected version as associated data, so diagnostics can explain the contract without logging the full document. ValidateSchema removes the first external label with an underscore, and its guard throws when the decision is reject. ValidatedBootstrap keeps the named label and default resource name from the loader. Both try expressions preserve their original failures because no broad catch erases them.

Add a second synthetic fixture with schemaVersion 2 to observe the opt-in through the integrated consumer. Its successful decoding alone should not bypass validation. Test a missing filename too, retaining ResourceFailure.missing. An unsupported schema and missing resource need different recovery: compatibility review versus packaging or lookup repair. The policy is intentionally not a complete schema migration engine and performs no persistence transformation; describe those limits explicitly.

sections.title: Write expected cases before checking the implementation
sections.html:
A decision table lists inputs and expected outcomes. Write it before the policy: version 1 accepts with opt-in false or true. Version 2 rejects with false and accepts with true. Versions -1, 0, and 3 reject in both states. These ten rows protect behavior rather than the shape of a switch. Then deliberately try a bad rule, such as accepting every version when opt-in is true. Predict which rows fail before restoring the correct rule.

The consumer matrix adds baseline fixture loading, typed missing-resource failure, unsupported-schema failure, and version-2 behavior under each effective condition selection. Test the public policy through an ordinary import from another module, because @testable alone can hide an accidental access-level problem. Report test methods and fixture rows separately: one looped XCTest method can cover ten decision rows without becoming ten discovered test functions.

Run only the isolated packages you created if your toolchain supports them. A paper trace is acceptable learning evidence when labeled as such. For a real dependency change, session 048's matrix would add affected retained and Tuist consumers, optimized linkage, resources, extensions, minimum-runtime cases, and specialist SDK checks as needed. No such production result follows from this scratch test. An unexpectedly broad pin diff, missing test discovery, or resource ownership change should stop acceptance until explained, rather than being covered by a green policy assertion.

sections.title: Rehearse both ways to restore the old behavior
sections.html:
Reconstruction means restoring the inputs and code needed for earlier behavior. The scratch lab has two paths. Removing the opt-in restores the old acceptance rule while leaving CoursePolicy available. Removing the dependency also requires restoring the previous consumer code and manifest edges. Record both and rerun baseline fixture and error cases. Reverting only a manifest line while keeping an import or validation call leaves a broken graph. Installed-client recovery is a further, separate question.

For a remote change, reconstruction additionally needs the prior manifest, relevant resolution file, selected revisions or binary checksums, generator/compiler versions, generated inputs, and resource contents. A signed archive is an artifact with its own identity, so rebuilding known-good source does not promise identical bytes. Preserve matching symbols and verification results for the candidate and the corrective build. Source rollback, binary reconstruction, and installed-client recovery are different claims.

For an App Store release, restoring old source is not a downgrade of installed clients. A correction requires a new version. Pausing phased updates limits further rollout; it does not undo already installed behavior. A runtime flag can contain only a path those clients already understand, with cached and offline limits. This scratch switch is compile-time, so changing it requires a rebuild. The release rehearsal records baseline and candidate evidence, unresolved reviews, containment limits, and the decision role. It performs no store operation.

sections.title: Submit the change with its evidence and limits
sections.html:
A review note should start with the observable behavior. Version 1 stays accepted. Version 2 needs explicit opt-in. Unknown versions still reject. Submit the scratch implementation or paper diff, package and target map, decision tables, and actual or predicted output. Then explain the separate compiler choice, unchanged resource owner, and preserved typed errors. A reviewer should be able to reproduce the rule and identify which consumer owns the opt-in from this note.

List limits alongside the result. This package has no remote supply chain, vendor binary, signing, UIKit screen, network cancellation, account storage, or database migration. Consequently its success cannot settle those specialist concerns. The active repository anchors show where real build conditions, generator inputs, and CI paths would need attention. They are review examples, not evidence that the client was changed or that its release artifact was validated.

Finally compare your explanation with the worked answer without marking the exercise complete automatically. If your implementation diverges, decide whether it satisfies the same acceptance contract and explain the tradeoff. A good reviewer should be able to reproduce the pure policy, identify the consumer that owns the opt-in, and reconstruct the baseline from your note. That completes this tooling unit's progression from naming build concepts to making a bounded, reviewable engineering decision.

exercise.solution:
Give CoursePolicy a library product that exposes its public source, plus a test target. Put the policy under Sources/CoursePolicy. The tests use ordinary import, so they check access from another module. @testable could hide a declaration that was accidentally left internal. The table inside the worked test covers five versions in two opt-in states. It checks behavior: schema 1 always accepts, schema 2 requires opt-in, and the other listed inputs reject. The manifest and test code below belong only to the scratch package.

// swift-tools-version: 5.9
import PackageDescription
let package = Package(
    name: "CoursePolicy",
    products: [
        .library(name: "CoursePolicy", targets: ["CoursePolicy"])
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(name: "CoursePolicy"),
        .testTarget(name: "CoursePolicyTests", dependencies: ["CoursePolicy"])
    ]
)
import XCTest
import CoursePolicy

final class PolicyContractTests: XCTestCase {
    func testSupportedAndUnknownVersions() {
        let cases: [(Int, Bool, SchemaDecision)] = [
            (-1, false, .reject), (-1, true, .reject),
            (0, false, .reject), (0, true, .reject),
            (1, false, .accept), (1, true, .accept),
            (2, false, .reject), (2, true, .accept),
            (3, false, .reject), (3, true, .reject)
        ]
        for (version, allowNext, expected) in cases {
            XCTAssertEqual(
                schemaDecision(for: version, allowNext: allowNext),
                expected,
                "version=\(version), opt-in=\(allowNext)"
            )
        }
    }
}

This is one discovered XCTest method with ten fixture rows. The consumer declaration and validator above complete the dependency seam. To opt in locally, add swiftSettings: [.define("COURSE_NEXT_SCHEMA")] to the scratch CourseResources production target, after its resource field; removing that setting restores the absent-condition branch. This is an independent lab condition, not an instruction to edit Debug or production settings in the client. Keep the consumer test target.

The schema-1 fixture passes validation in both builds. A schema-2 fixture rejects without the condition and accepts with it. The missing-name path still throws ResourceFailure.missing, and corrupt JSON still fails decoding. For a loader-independent error assertion, call validateSchema(2, allowNext: false) and check the unsupportedSchema associated value. The deliberate accept-everything mutation fails invalid/future opt-in rows.

Reconstruction first removes the scratch define and reruns baseline behavior. Complete dependency removal also restores pre-change consumer code and removes the local package/product/import together. A real remote rollback would restore the relevant pins and artifact inputs. In the tabletop release note, compiler-condition changes require a new build, runtime containment has explicit limits, and installed App Store clients require a corrective release. All actual client, device, archive, distribution, licensing, and security checks remain pending.

simple.story: Ben runs a club library. Members normally borrow books with blue labels. The club tries a second shelf with green labels. A written trial card says whether that shelf is open today. Ben still rejects books with red labels, even when the trial is open. Closing the trial shelf restores the old borrowing rule. Removing the whole shelf is a different job: Ben must also remove its catalogue entry and signs so nobody follows directions to a shelf that is gone.
